name: Professional extractions / acne facial

lead: Professional extraction is manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads by an esthetician or dermatologist, often during an acne facial. The payoff is visibly cleaner pores and smoother-looking skin right after the session.

A comedo is a follicle clogged with keratin and oil, either open (a blackhead) or closed (a whitehead). A comedo extractor applies pressure to expel the plug, usually after steaming or warm washing. Open comedones are generally easier to remove than closed ones. It is standard acne facial practice, though the sources found no controlled trials specific to it.

paras: People book it as a periodic facial or dermatology visit, often combined with a home routine for keeping pores clear. Results in the pores are visible immediately.
Picking or squeezing risks infection and scarring, so hygiene and technique matter. A poorly done extraction can leave marks.

chain: Manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads
angle.text: A professional manually clears blackheads and whiteheads, giving visibly cleaner pores right after the session. It is standard acne facial practice, with little formal trial evidence on long-term outcomes.

lead: Professional comedone extraction is the manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads by an esthetician or dermatologist, usually as part of an acne facial. People use it to clear clogged pores that make skin look rough, dotted or congested, and to get a smoother, clearer surface without the damage that can come from squeezing at home.[1]

A comedo is a hair follicle plugged with keratin and oil. It is open (a blackhead, dark because of oxidation rather than dirt) or closed (a whitehead).[1] Dermatologists can often remove open comedones with little trauma to the skin, while closed ones are harder to extract.[1] Salons and clinics use comedo extractors and typically steam the face or wash it with warm water first, with attention to hygiene.[1]

Published trials of esthetician extractions themselves are not available; the practice is described mainly in dermatology references and encyclopedic summaries, alongside research on related acne and pore-care products.[1][2]

paras: Comedo extractors are used in salons and by dermatologists, normally after steaming the face or washing with warm water.[1] Open comedones tend to come out with minimal skin trauma, whereas closed comedones are harder to remove.[1]

Larger comedones of about 1 mm or more (macrocomedones) may be removed with surgical instruments or cauterised with a light-based device. Because isotretinoin can cause severe flare-ups of these lesions, dermatologists often remove them before and during that treatment.[1]
Dermatologists can also use cyanoacrylate to lift blackheads across an area, a stronger method than over-the-counter pore strips, which are gentler but can still damage skin.[1]

Extraction is one of several ways comedones are managed. Others include topical retinoids and azelaic acid, which Wikipedia notes appear beneficial without increasing pigmentation, and laser treatment, which may reduce comedones although lasers and dermabrasion have been known to cause scarring.[1]

Dermatology literature on post-acne marks notes that lesions that have been traumatised are a recognised risk factor for acne-induced hyperpigmentation, particularly in people with darker skin tones, which is one reason skin-care discussions emphasise gentle handling of lesions.[3]

In appearance communities, professional extractions are discussed as a periodic facial for blackheads and congestion and as a substitute for self-squeezing. Community discussion centres on skin clarity and on avoiding the marks and scars that picking can leave.

Squeezing or picking can damage the skin, raise the risk of infection and scarring, and may push infection deeper.[1] Pore strips may leave pores open and remove surface skin, and dermabrasion and laser can cause scarring.[1] Excessive washing or scrubbing can irritate skin and worsen comedones.[1]

No studies found. Related clinical research has examined topical products for oily skin, blackheads and enlarged pores; one 56-day trial evaluated an emulsion containing niacinamide and plant extracts for acne and conspicuous pores, but it did not test manual extraction.[2]

lore.intro: Extractions come up in skin-care discussion as the professional alternative to squeezing at home.[1]

claims.claim: Professional extraction is gentler on skin than squeezing at home.
A facial can clear blackheads without further treatment.
